title: A search trace shows where an optimiser looked; the surface is only the part you can draw honestly
summary: Height-map surfaces exist for exactly two inputs and one output. These figures show a CMA-ES search through the surface for two variables, through a coloured point cloud for three, and through a fixed slice for three: each is an honest answer to a different dimension problem.

media.alt: Left: a 3D surface of log10(1 + f) for the Rosenbrock function over x1 from -2 to 2 and x2 from about -1 to 3, a curved valley, with red dots scattered along it and a yellow marker near the bottom. Right: a line chart of best objective value on a log axis from about 5 down to 1e-12 against evaluations so far from 0 to 2300, flat at first and then falling steeply after about 700.

source.caption: Rosenbrock: watch the search itself, not a spinning camera
group: 10_10_surface_trace_3d_poster: CMA-ES on Rosenbrock, fixed camera, evaluation cloud on the surface and the best-so-far panel at 2300 of 2300 evaluations, final value 2.921e-17 (representative; a video, this page uses its poster frame)
11_11_surface_himmelblau_poster: the same treatment on Himmelblau, which has four equal-depth minima; 655 of 655 evaluations, final value 2.239e-18 (video poster frame)
07_07_threevar_trajectory_poster: every evaluation of a 3-variable CMA-ES run as a point at its own (x1, x2, x3), colour = objective on a log scale, red line = best-so-far path (video poster frame)
12_12_threevar_surface_slice: a fixed-slice surface at x3 = 1.000 with the run's (x1, x2) path projected onto it, point colour = true 3D objective
source.note: The three-variable objective is not named on the figures. Only what is drawn is described here.

read_the_figure.question: Where did the search go, how fast did the best value fall, and how much of the landscape does this picture truly show?
read_the_figure.axes: Left of the representative figure: x1 and x2 are the two decision variables; the vertical axis is log10(1 + f), a compressed objective, with f = 0 at height 0. Right panel: evaluations so far (linear) against best objective value (log). In the 3-variable figure, all three axes are decision variables, and colour carries the objective on a log scale. In the slice figure, height is the objective with x3 frozen at 1.000, and colour is the true 3D objective.
look_at: Red dots are evaluations, not a continuous path. A dense cluster means the search spent many evaluations there; a thin spray means broad exploration.
The yellow marker is the current best. Follow it to see which valley the run committed to.
On the right panel, a flat stretch followed by a steep fall means the search was exploring or adapting its sampling shape before it found the valley floor.
In the Himmelblau figure, count the dips on the surface: four, and the run ends in one of them. The others are equally good, so the choice among them is not an error.
In the 3-variable point cloud, a surface cannot be drawn: look at the colour. The cloud contracts onto one point as the run converges.
In the slice figure, the points hover above or below the surface: that is expected, because their colour reports the true 3D value while the height reports the frozen slice.
read_the_figure.proves: Where this particular run sampled and how its best value evolved. It does not map the full landscape, and in three variables the slice shows only a two-dimensional cut through it.
if_wrong: A cloud that stays spread out and a best-value curve that stays flat: the search did not find a valley within the budget.
Points that fall far outside the plotted box: the figure's axis limits hide part of the run.
A slice read as the real landscape: valleys in the slice can be shallower or deeper than in the full space.
must_check: The vertical axis says what is plotted (log10(1 + f), not f), because the compression flattens enormous heights.
The camera is fixed or stated; rotating views make comparison between frames impossible.
The objective colour scale is labelled and on a log axis.
For more than two variables: a statement of what is held fixed in any surface shown (here x3 = 1.000).
The number of evaluations is stated (2300/2300 and 655/655 are in the figure titles).
as_drawn: Values in the figures: Rosenbrock CMA-ES final best 2.921e-17 after 2300 evaluations (title and axis); Himmelblau 2.239e-18 after 655 evaluations. The Rosenbrock number matches the same solver's entry in the solver-race scoreboard.

The Rosenbrock best-value curve is flat near 5 for the first roughly 700 evaluations (read by eye), then falls about thirteen decades by about 2100. The Himmelblau run falls much sooner, from the start to about 1e-4 within roughly 120 evaluations (read by eye).

Slice figure: x3 = 1.000. Two dips are visible on the surface, one deeper at the right. Colour bar runs 0 to about 3,600 for the true objective, so the red points at the edges are far from any minimum.
3-variable cloud: colour bar spans about 1e-9 (yellow) to 1e3 (purple), and the red best-so-far line makes a few long jumps before it settles at the yellow marker near the middle.

terms.meaning: An input the optimiser is free to change. The dimension of the problem is the number of decision variables.
The graph of f over two decision variables: height is f. It exists only for two inputs and one output.
A monotone, compressive transform: it keeps order, maps f = 0 to 0 and flattens huge values, so a banana valley with values over 1000 can be drawn.
A standard test function with four equal minima of value 0.
A lower-dimensional cut of a function obtained by fixing some variables. Here x3 is fixed so that (x1, x2) can be drawn as a surface.
An evolution strategy that samples a cloud around a mean and adapts the cloud's shape to the landscape; the cloud of red dots is its samples.
A view that does not rotate during the animation, so frames can be compared directly.

remember: A surface plot needs exactly two inputs; with three or more you must show a cloud, a slice, or a projection and say which.
log10(1 + f) preserves ordering but not ratios: heights are not proportional to f.
Equal minima are all correct answers; a run that picks one is not wrong.
Dots are samples, not a trajectory: the path is only the best-so-far line.
Colour and height in the slice figure encode different quantities on purpose.

understand.title: Why the surface needs a transform
understand.text: Rosenbrock reaches values in the thousands at the corners and zero at the valley floor. On a linear height axis the floor would be indistinguishable from zero everywhere. Taking log10(1 + f) leaves the floor at zero, brings the corners to a few units, and keeps the valley visible.

understand.title: Why a slice is not the landscape
understand.text: Freezing x3 at 1.000 picks one two-dimensional cut. The search path projected onto it visits points whose true x3 differs from 1, so their true objective values differ from the surface height under them. The figure shows both quantities, which is why colour and height disagree.

steps.title: Four minima of Himmelblau, checked
steps.note: The point (3, 2) is one of four exact zeros; the others are near (-2.81, 3.13), (-3.78, -3.28) and (3.58, -1.85). Substituting (3, 2) gives zero in both brackets, which is the exact check; the other three are the standard numerical values.

steps.title: The plotted height
steps.note: Since f is non-negative for these test functions, z is zero exactly at a global minimum, and increases with f. Equal steps in z are ten-fold steps in 1 + f.

steps.title: A slice of a three-variable function
steps.note: The surface in the slice figure is g. A point of the search path has true value f(x1, x2, x3), which equals g(x1, x2) only when its x3 equals x3*. That is why the figure's title states the quantities are deliberately different.

steps.title: Best-so-far from the samples
steps.note: The right panel and the red path both show this running minimum, not the individual samples. It is monotone, so a plateau means no new sample improved on the best.

steps.title: Why the sampling cloud contracts
steps.note: CMA-ES samples from a Gaussian whose step size sigma and covariance C adapt. As the search converges, sigma shrinks, so the dots crowd onto the optimum, which is the dense core visible in the 3-variable cloud.

worked.title: How many decades did the best value fall?
worked.problem: Rosenbrock panel: the best value is about 5 when it starts to fall and the title gives the final value 2.921e-17. How many decades is that?

solution.text: Take the base-10 logarithm of the ratio.
Note that the log axis of the panel is cut off at 1e-12, so the last five decades are not visible.

worked.answer: About 17 decades from the plateau value to the final value, although the panel is drawn only to 1e-12, so the plotted curve shows about 13 of them. The starting value of 5 is read by eye.

analyze.q: The Himmelblau run ends in one of four equal minima. What would you need to know to say which one a given run will pick?
analyze.hint: Start point, initial step size and random seed.

analyze.q: In the slice figure the dots sit above and below the surface. Is that evidence of a plotting error?
analyze.hint: Which variable is not on the axes?

analyze.q: The Rosenbrock best-value curve stays flat for about 700 evaluations. List two reasons a population method can stall that long before the valley is found.
analyze.hint: Step size adaptation and the covariance matrix starting spherical.

evaluate.q: Is a 3D surface with a trace better than a contour map with a trace for these two-variable problems? Name one advantage and one cost of the surface.
evaluate.hint: Occlusion, perspective, readability of the path.

evaluate.q: A viewer takes the 3-variable cloud as proof that the optimum found is global. What does the figure not show?
evaluate.hint: One run, no restarts, no map of the rest of the space.

create: Draw the Himmelblau search as a contour map with the four minima marked and the run's final point labelled with its distance to each minimum.
Design a figure for a four-variable problem that keeps honesty about what is shown: which two views would you choose and what would you state in the title?

checks.q: Why plot log10(1 + f) rather than f?
checks.hint: Large dynamic range and f = 0 at the minimum.
checks.answer: Because f spans from zero to thousands. The transform keeps the floor at zero, compresses the large values so the whole surface is visible, and preserves ordering.

checks.q: What is z = log10(1 + f) when f = 99?
Why can there not be a single height-map surface for a three-variable objective?
checks.answer: A height map uses two axes for inputs and one for the output. With three inputs plus the output you need four dimensions, so you must slice, project or colour instead.

checks.q: Himmelblau has four equal minima. Is a run that finds one of them a failure?
checks.answer: No. Each is a global minimum with the same value, so any of them is a correct answer. Which one is found depends on the start and the random seed.

checks.q: How would you show the dependence of the end point on the start for Himmelblau?
checks.answer: Run from a grid of starting points and colour each point on the plane by which of the four minima the run reached, which gives a basin-of-attraction map.
